nameStory: This mushroom gets its quirky name 'hen of the woods' because its overlapping, ruffled caps look remarkably like the feathers of a fluffed-up hen sitting at the base of a tree. Some folks also call it 'sheep's head' or 'ram's head' for the same fluffy, layered appearance. In Japan, it's known as 'maitake' meaning 'dancing mushroom' — legend says people would dance with joy when they found this prized edible!
description: Hen of the woods is a spectacular mushroom that looks like a giant brown flower blooming at the base of trees. Instead of a typical mushroom cap and stem, it forms massive clusters of overlapping, fan-shaped caps that can grow as large as a basketball or even bigger. Each individual cap is grayish-brown on top with a paler underside, and the whole cluster emerges from a branching white base. This is a polypore mushroom, meaning it has tiny pores instead of gills underneath its caps.

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms large, rosette-like clusters at the base of trees with dozens of overlapping, fan-shaped caps branching from a central white base — unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Individual caps are grayish-brown to dark brown on top, often with darker edges, feeling slightly velvety when young and becoming tougher with age

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Undersides have tiny white to cream-colored pores instead of gills — run your finger along them and they feel smooth with barely visible holes

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: No traditional stem — instead has thick, white, branching stalks that connect all the caps together like tree branches

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, earthy, slightly nutty aroma — if it smells sour or unpleasant, it's past its prime

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: May darken slightly when cut or bruised, and the pore surface can yellow with age or handling

habitat: Look for hen of the woods at the base of large, mature oak and maple trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It's most common in areas with old-growth trees or forests that have been undisturbed for many years, as it prefers trees that are at least several decades old. You'll find it growing directly from the soil around tree roots, often in the same spots year after year.

seasonality.spring: No visible mushrooms in spring, though the underground mycelium is active and growing through the root systems of host trees.
seasonality.summer: Occasionally fruits in late summer after heavy rains, but these early specimens are less common in New England.
seasonality.fall: Peak season! September through October brings the best fruiting, especially after warm, wet periods. Look for fresh clusters that feel firm and smell pleasant.
seasonality.winter: Old, dried specimens may persist on trees, appearing dark and leathery, but no fresh mushrooms emerge in winter cold.

funFact: A single hen of the woods cluster can weigh over 50 pounds and contain enough mushroom to feed a small army — some record specimens have tipped the scales at over 100 pounds, making them among the largest mushrooms you can find in New England!
confusionNotes: Young specimens might be confused with Berkeley's polypore, but Berkeley's grows on dead wood and has a more shelf-like appearance rather than the rosette pattern. Remember: hen of the woods grows from soil at the base of living trees in a circular, flower-like cluster, while shelf fungi grow directly out of tree trunks in overlapping brackets.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its many common names (hen of the woods, sheep's head, ram's head), this is completely different from 'chicken of the woods' — a bright yellow and orange shelf mushroom. The 'maitake' you might see in grocery stores is this same species, commercially cultivated and prized for its meaty texture and rich flavor.
compareHints: Hen of the woods is the only Grifola species you'll encounter in New England, making it unique in its genus here. It differs from other large polypores like Berkeley's polypore by its ground-growing habit and rosette formation, and from oyster mushrooms by its pore surface instead of gills. The branching, clustered growth pattern from a soil base is truly distinctive among New England fungi.
